title: Searching and Sorting Algorithms
intro: An **algorithm** is a step-by-step recipe. Searching and sorting are the classics: they show how the same answer can take very different amounts of work. **Linear search** checks every item; **binary search** halves a *sorted* list each step, so a million items take about 20 checks. We describe growth with **Big-O**: O(n) grows with the list, O(log n) barely grows, O(n²) explodes.

questions.prompt: Binary search keeps a window `lo..hi` and looks at the middle. Too small? Search the right half. Too big? The left half.
questions.explanation: Twenty-ish steps for a million items — that's O(log n).

questions.prompt: Write `linear_search(items, target)` that returns the index of the first `target` in `items`, or `-1` if it isn't there. Use a loop, not `.index()`.

tests.name: found
tests.code: assert linear_search([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42], 16) == 3 and linear_search(['a', 'b', 'a'], 'a') == 0, 'Return the index of the first match.'

tests.name: missing
tests.code: assert linear_search([1, 2, 3], 9) == -1 and linear_search([], 1) == -1, 'Return -1 when the target is missing.'

tests.name: no index()
tests.code: assert 'index' not in linear_search.__code__.co_names, 'Write the loop yourself instead of calling .index().'

questions.hint: `enumerate` gives each index with its item.
questions.explanation: Linear search works on any list, sorted or not, but checks up to n items: O(n).

questions.prompt: Write `binary_search(items, target)` for a **sorted** list. Return the index of `target`, or `-1`. Don't use `.index()` or `in`.

tests.name: found
tests.code:
data = list(range(3, 300, 3))
assert all(binary_search(data, x) == i for i, x in enumerate(data)), 'Every item should be found at its index.'

tests.name: missing
tests.code: assert binary_search([1, 3, 5, 7], 4) == -1 and binary_search([], 1) == -1 and binary_search([2], 1) == -1, 'Missing targets return -1.'

tests.name: fast

questions.hint: Keep `lo` and `hi`; look at `mid = (lo + hi) // 2`; move one end past `mid`.
questions.explanation: The `lo <= hi` condition and `mid ± 1` updates are where off-by-one bugs hide. Test with 0, 1 and 2 items.

questions.prompt: Binary search needs the list to be…
questions.hint: How does it decide which half to keep?
questions.explanation: It compares with the middle item to throw away half — that only works if the order is known.

questions.prompt: The standard library has binary search in `bisect`. What does this print?
questions.code:
import bisect

scores = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(bisect.bisect_left(scores, 25), bisect.bisect_left(scores, 30))
bisect.insort(scores, 25)
print(scores)
questions.hint: `bisect_left` gives the position where the value would go.
questions.explanation: 25 would go at index 2; 30 is already at index 2. `insort` inserts while keeping the list sorted.

questions.prompt: Write `bubble_sort(items)` that returns a **new** sorted list using bubble sort: repeatedly swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. Stop early when a pass makes no swaps. Don't call `sorted` or `.sort()`.

tests.name: sorts
tests.code:
import random as _r
_data = [_r.Random(7).randint(0, 99) for _ in range(40)]
assert bubble_sort(_data) == sorted(_data) and bubble_sort([]) == [] and bubble_sort([3, 1, 2, 1]) == [1, 1, 2, 3], 'The result should be sorted.'

tests.name: new list
tests.code:
_x = [3, 1, 2]
bubble_sort(_x)
assert _x == [3, 1, 2], 'Do not change the original list.'

tests.name: own code
tests.code: assert not {'sorted', 'sort'} & set(bubble_sort.__code__.co_names), 'Write the sorting loops yourself.'

questions.hint: Copy with `list(items)`. An outer loop for passes, an inner loop comparing `result[i]` and `result[i + 1]`.
questions.explanation: Bubble sort is O(n²): fine for 20 items, hopeless for a million. Its early stop makes it fast on lists that are already sorted.

questions.prompt: Write `merge_sorted(a, b)` that merges two **sorted** lists into one sorted list in a single pass (no `sorted`). This is the heart of merge sort.

tests.name: merge
tests.code: assert merge_sorted([1, 4, 9], [2, 3, 10, 11]) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11], 'Merge both lists in order.'

tests.name: edges
tests.code: assert merge_sorted([], [1, 2]) == [1, 2] and merge_sorted([5], []) == [5] and merge_sorted([1, 1], [1]) == [1, 1, 1], 'Handle empty lists and duplicates.'

tests.name: no sorted
tests.code: assert not {'sorted', 'sort'} & set(merge_sorted.__code__.co_names), 'Merge with two positions instead of sorting.'

questions.hint: Keep a position in each list; append the smaller front item; add whatever is left at the end.
questions.explanation: Each item is looked at once, so merging is O(n).

questions.prompt: Now write `merge_sort(items)`: split the list in half, sort each half with `merge_sort`, then combine them with `merge_sorted` (already defined for you).

tests.name: sorts
tests.code:
import random as _r
_g = _r.Random(3)
for _n in (0, 1, 2, 7, 64):
    _data = [_g.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(_n)]
    assert merge_sort(_data) == sorted(_data), f'merge_sort should sort a list of {_n} items.'

tests.name: recursive
tests.code: assert 'merge_sort' in merge_sort.__code__.co_names and not {'sorted', 'sort'} & set(merge_sort.__code__.co_names), 'merge_sort should call itself on each half, without sorted().'

questions.hint: Base case: 0 or 1 items are already sorted. Otherwise split at `len(items) // 2`.
questions.explanation: Splitting gives log n levels, and each level merges n items: O(n log n) — the same growth as Python's own `sorted`.

questions.prompt: Sorting 1,000,000 numbers: which is fastest in practice?
questions.explanation: `sorted` (Timsort) is O(n log n) like merge sort but written in C and tuned for real data. Write your own to learn; use `sorted` in real code.

questions.prompt: Use the right tool: given a list of `(name, score)` pairs, write `top_three(results)` returning the three names with the highest scores, highest first. Ties keep alphabetical order.

tests.name: top
tests.code: assert top_three([('Ana', 71), ('Ben', 93), ('Caro', 88), ('Dev', 93), ('Eli', 40)]) == ['Ben', 'Dev', 'Caro'], 'Highest scores first; ties alphabetical.'

tests.name: short
tests.code: assert top_three([('Solo', 5)]) == ['Solo'], 'Fewer than three results is fine.'

questions.hint: Sort with a key of `(-score, name)` and slice the first three.
questions.explanation: A negative score sorts high scores first while names still sort A–Z within a tie.
